evidence_window: Resource snapshots 6 Nov 2026; sign-ins 2 of 2 days archived; Windows audit 1 of 30 days archived
headline: {TENANT} faces about {ALE} of expected cyber loss a year, and a bad year could exceed {P90}
summary: Using FAIR-style analysis calibrated with {TENANT}’s own security telemetry, we estimate expected annual cyber loss at {ALE}, with a 1-in-10-year loss of {P90} and a 1-in-20-year loss of {P95}. {TOP_NAME} is the largest exposure, about {TOP_SHARE} of expected loss. {FREQ_NAME} is the most likely to occur in any year. The recommended actions cut expected loss to {TALE}, an avoided loss of about {SAVED} a year. Where the telemetry cannot measure a control, the ranges are widened, never reduced.
board_ask: accept this quantified view as the basis for cyber investment decisions, approve the highest-return actions first, and confirm whether a 1-in-10-year loss of {P90} is within the organization’s tolerance.

scenarios.name: Ransomware & operational extortion
scenarios.description: Encryption of servers and endpoints, with possible data theft, halting operations.
evidence: 6 backup servers on a build with a critical flaw (CVE-2025-48983, CVE-2025-48984) and joined to the production domain
167 active devices have no EDR agent, including 5 servers and 9 end-of-life systems
19 anti-ransomware hardening rules reported as failing on every assessed device
788 of 788 EDR agents are not fully in Protect mode
369 devices carry an exploitable vulnerability older than 30 days
Log clearing
14 endpoints run remote-access tools outside the sanctioned set
Not measurable: backup success, age, immutability and restore tests cannot be measured, so recovery ability is unproven
Not measurable: no Windows audit archive, so log clearing and persistence are unknown
scenarios.calibration: Baseline frequency for a mid-market organization is 0.08 events a year; the most likely value rises above the baseline because of exposed backup servers, devices without endpoint protection, anti-ransomware hardening not confirmed. The range is widened by 20% at the top end because 2 inputs cannot be measured. Per-event cost is anchored to the IBM 2025 average cost of a ransomware or extortion incident ($5.08M) and scaled to organization size.

scenarios.name: Business email compromise & payment fraud
scenarios.description: A compromised or spoofed mailbox redirects a payment or invoice.
evidence: 35.5% of successful sign-ins were single-factor (7,348 of 20,688, 3 days)
No enforced conditional-access policy requires MFA for all users on all apps
36 legacy-authentication sign-ins, which cannot use MFA
61 sign-ins flagged risky
7,865 of 28,553 sign-in attempts failed, a pattern consistent with password attacks
1,523 inbox-rule changes over 3 archived days, up to 1,011 in one day; mail-client syncs are included, so this raises frequency only modestly
46 mailbox-permission changes over 3 archived days

Not measurable: the destination of forwards, who made rule changes and payment-verification controls cannot be measured (the archive counts changes, not their content, and rules saved by an Outlook client carry no detail)
Not measurable: forwarding changes are not in the archive (the archived script predates the counter)
scenarios.calibration: Baseline frequency for a mid-market organization is 0.5 events a year; the most likely value rises above the baseline because of single-factor sign-ins, no all-users MFA, legacy authentication in use. The range is widened by 20% at the top end because 2 inputs cannot be measured. Per-event loss uses the FBI IC3 average BEC loss (about $130K) with a long tail for large wires.

scenarios.calibration: Baseline frequency for a mid-market organization is 0.1 events a year; the most likely value rises above the baseline because of single-factor sign-ins, no all-users MFA, risky sign-ins. The range is widened by 20% at the top end because 2 inputs cannot be measured. Per-event cost sits below the IBM 2025 global average breach ($4.44M) at mid-market scale, with a tail toward the US average ($10.22M).

treatments.name: Patch and isolate backup servers; immutable copies
treatments.detail: Upgrade the backup software to a fixed build, move backup servers out of the production domain and keep an immutable or offline copy.

treatments.name: Prove recovery: restore test and backup monitoring
treatments.detail: Run and record a restore test of the critical systems and send backup job results to the SIEM so recovery ability can be measured.

treatments.name: Close endpoint gaps and turn on anti-ransomware hardening
treatments.detail: EDR on the 167 unprotected devices, Protect mode on every agent, ASR rules, LAPS and Credential Guard.

treatments.name: Patch exploitable vulnerabilities, oldest first
treatments.detail: Close the 369 devices with exploitable vulnerabilities older than 30 days.

treatments.name: Enforce MFA and Conditional Access
treatments.detail: Enforce MFA for every administrator and every user, remove role exclusions and move toward phishing-resistant methods.

treatments.name: Payment verification and inbox-rule alerting
treatments.detail: Out-of-band verification for bank-detail changes; alert on new forwarding and inbox rules. Confirm whether this is already in place.

treatments.name: Stop log clearing; keep 90-day log retention
treatments.detail: Archive instead of clear; forward all domain-controller events to the SIEM.

assumptions: No revenue or downtime cost was supplied, so business interruption is scaled from a reference organization of 1,700 accounts. Replace with the organization’s own figures to sharpen the estimate.
Loss per event is scaled to about 1,761 enabled accounts using the square root of size against a 1,700-account reference organization, limited to between 0.3 and 3 times the reference.
Cyber insurance recoveries and deductibles are not netted off; losses are gross.
Extortion payment is modelled as usually not paid (most likely $0), consistent with IBM 2025 reporting that most victims refuse to pay.
Annual control costs were not supplied, so return on investment is not calculated: cost to be supplied.
Treatment effects are expert estimates of how much each control reduces frequency or cost, not measurements.

Accidental and insider data exposure, including shadow AI, is not modelled: the Office 365 archive counts sharing and external-access events but shows zero DLP matches, which cannot separate "no DLP policy" from "no matches", and there is no generative-AI egress source.
Third-party and remote-tool compromise is not modelled separately to avoid double counting; extra remote-access tools already raise the ransomware frequency.

Frequency and cost ranges come from fixed calibration rules (references/calibration_rules.md), applied to the ransomware-readiness evidence (Resource snapshots 6 Nov 2026; sign-ins 2 of 2 days archived; Windows audit 1 of 30 days archived).
sources: IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025: global average breach $4.44M; US average $10.22M; ransomware or extortion incident $5.08M; shadow AI adds about $670K
FBI IC3 Internet Crime Report (BEC loss per complaint, approximate)
The Open Group Risk Taxonomy (O-RT) and Risk Analysis (O-RA) standards (FAIR)
